text: A cruise ship. A daycare in February. A house where everyone got the same stomach bug, except one person.
Sometimes that person just got lucky. And occasionally, luck isn't the whole explanation.

Norovirus can't push its way into you. It has to grab onto a specific sugar coating on the cells lining your gut. And a gene called F U T two is what builds that coating. In people whose F U T two is switched off, the coating is never made.
The virus arrives at a door with no handle.
Danish researchers followed real outbreaks of the most common norovirus strain. Among people carrying two broken copies, symptomatic infection essentially didn't happen.
A gene that quit, working as the most effective bouncer in the building.
About one in five people of European ancestry carries two broken copies.
The fine print is real, and there are two.

One. Non-secretors carry a higher risk of Crohn's disease. Two. They also carry a higher risk of type one diabetes. That sugar coating isn't only a handle for viruses. It also feeds bacteria your gut depends on.
And against several other norovirus strains, the door opens fine.
So if you're ever the only one still eating, you might know who to thank. Just don't get cocky.
